skill_title: Use standard electrode potentials to predict and calculate cell EMF
notes: 20 items: 8 lifted, 12 fresh. Standard E° values: predict spontaneity, identify oxidising/reducing agents, calculate E°_cell = E°_cathode − E°_anode.

items.question: State the STANDARD CONDITIONS for measuring standard electrode potentials.
items.expectedAnswer: Standard conditions: temperature = 25°C (298 K); all aqueous concentrations = 1 mol·dm⁻³; pressure of any gases = 101.3 kPa (1 atm); pure substances (e.g. metal electrodes) in their standard state.
items.explanation: Standard state: 1 M, 1 atm, 298 K, pure solids/liquids.

items.question: Calculate the EMF of the galvanic cell Pb | Pb²⁺ || Fe³⁺, Fe²⁺ | Pt at standard conditions. (E°(Pb²⁺/Pb) = −0.13 V; E°(Fe³⁺/Fe²⁺) = +0.77 V.)
items.explanation: Anode (left) = Pb (more negative E°). Cathode (right) = Fe³⁺/Fe²⁺. E°_cell = E°_cathode − E°_anode = +0.77 − (−0.13) = +0.90 V.

items.question: A galvanic cell uses Hg|Hg²⁺ (E° = +0.85 V) as one half-cell. Which OTHER half-cell will give the HIGHEST cell EMF?
items.explanation: Hg is the cathode (highest E°). The anode should have the MOST NEGATIVE E° to maximise (E°_cathode − E°_anode). Li gives the largest EMF.

items.question: A galvanic cell has an Al rod (E°(Al³⁺/Al) = −1.66 V) and a half-cell involving an unknown gas X. The cell EMF is +2.89 V. Use standard electrode potentials to find E° for X (it's the cathode).
items.explanation: E°_cell = E°_cathode − E°_anode = E°_X − (−1.66) = E°_X + 1.66 = 2.89 ⇒ E°_X = +1.23 V. This matches the O₂/H₂O electrode in acidic solution. So X = O₂.

items.question: Calculate the EMF of the galvanic cell Zn | Zn²⁺ || Cu²⁺ | Cu. (E°(Zn²⁺/Zn) = −0.76 V; E°(Cu²⁺/Cu) = +0.34 V.)
items.explanation: Zn is anode (more negative E°). Cu is cathode. E°_cell = 0.34 − (−0.76) = +1.10 V (positive ⇒ spontaneous).

items.question: A galvanic cell has E°_cell = −0.50 V. What does this tell you about the reaction as written?
items.expectedAnswer: Negative E°_cell means the reaction as written is NON-SPONTANEOUS. The cell would not operate spontaneously in this direction. If we reverse the reaction (swap anode and cathode), the magnitude becomes +0.50 V, which is the spontaneous direction.
items.explanation: Sign of E°_cell predicts spontaneity. Positive ⇒ spontaneous (galvanic). Negative ⇒ non-spontaneous (requires electrolysis to run).

items.question: In a cell consisting of an Al electrode and an O₂/H⁺ electrode, identify the REDUCING agent.
items.expectedAnswer: Al (aluminium). Al is oxidised at the anode (loses electrons: Al → Al³⁺ + 3e⁻); the species that is oxidised IS the reducing agent (it reduces the other species by donating electrons).
items.explanation: Reducing agent = species that gets oxidised (loses electrons to reduce something else).

items.question: An electrode X gains mass when connected to a standard hydrogen electrode (SHE). EMF = +1.20 V. Identify X. (E°(SHE) = 0 V.)
items.expectedAnswer: X gains mass ⇒ X is the cathode (M²⁺ + 2e⁻ → M deposits). E°_cell = E°_X − 0 = +1.20 V ⇒ E°_X = +1.20 V. From the standard table, the electrode with E° ≈ +1.20 V matches Au³⁺/Au (≈ +1.50 V) is too high; +1.20 V is unusual — could be a custom or approximate value matching the question's standard table. The exact identification depends on the table provided.
items.explanation: Cathode = mass gain. E°_cell = E°_X (since SHE is 0). Look up E° = +1.20 V in the standard table.

items.question: Arrange Au³⁺ (E° = +1.50 V), H⁺ (E° = 0.00 V), and Zn²⁺ (E° = −0.76 V) as OXIDISING AGENTS from STRONGEST to WEAKEST.
items.expectedAnswer: Strongest to weakest oxidising agent: Au³⁺ > H⁺ > Zn²⁺. More positive E° ⇒ more easily reduced ⇒ stronger oxidising agent.
items.explanation: Higher E° = stronger oxidiser (better at gaining electrons). Reverse order for reducing-agent strength.

items.question: From the table of standard electrode potentials, which has the STRONGEST reducing agent: Na (E° = −2.71 V), Mg (−2.38 V), Zn (−0.76 V), Cu (+0.34 V)?
items.explanation: Strongest reducing agent has the MOST NEGATIVE E° (most easily oxidised). Na has the most negative E° among these ⇒ strongest reducing agent.

items.question: A learner reverses a reduction half-reaction (writes it as an oxidation) and CHANGES the sign of E°. Is this correct?
items.expectedAnswer: When writing the formula E°_cell = E°_cathode − E°_anode, you should use the REDUCTION POTENTIAL values from the table for BOTH half-reactions (don't change signs). However, if you want the actual potential for an oxidation (e.g. as a 'half-cell potential' in another convention), then yes, the sign reverses. Be careful with whichever convention you use.
items.explanation: CAPS convention: use reduction potentials in E°_cell = E°_cath − E°_anode. Don't flip signs.

items.question: Determine the EMF of a cell with the reaction 3Sn²⁺ + 2Al → 3Sn + 2Al³⁺. (E°(Sn²⁺/Sn) = −0.14 V; E°(Al³⁺/Al) = −1.66 V.)
items.explanation: Sn²⁺ is reduced (cathode); Al is oxidised (anode). E°_cell = E°_cathode − E°_anode = −0.14 − (−1.66) = +1.52 V. Positive ⇒ spontaneous.

items.question: A Ni²⁺ solution needs to be stored in a metal container. Should COPPER or ZINC be used? Explain using standard electrode potentials. (E°(Cu²⁺/Cu) = +0.34 V; E°(Zn²⁺/Zn) = −0.76 V; E°(Ni²⁺/Ni) = −0.27 V.)
items.expectedAnswer: Use COPPER. The container will be safe if its metal is a WEAKER reducing agent than the metal in solution. Copper (E° = +0.34 V) is a weaker reducing agent than Ni (E° = −0.27 V), so Cu will NOT reduce Ni²⁺ — no reaction. Zinc (E° = −0.76 V) is a STRONGER reducing agent than Ni, so Zn would react with Ni²⁺ (Zn + Ni²⁺ → Zn²⁺ + Ni), corroding the container.
items.explanation: Compare E°: the container must have HIGHER (more positive) E° than the ion in solution to avoid being oxidised.

items.question: Will the reaction Cu + 2H⁺ → Cu²⁺ + H₂ occur spontaneously at standard conditions? (E°(Cu²⁺/Cu) = +0.34 V; E°(2H⁺/H₂) = 0.00 V.)
items.expectedAnswer: No. For the reaction as written, Cu is oxidised (anode, E° = +0.34 V) and H⁺ is reduced (cathode, E° = 0). E°_cell = 0 − 0.34 = −0.34 V (NEGATIVE) ⇒ NON-spontaneous. Copper does NOT react with dilute acid (e.g. HCl). The reverse direction is spontaneous, but the forward is not.
items.explanation: Negative E°_cell ⇒ non-spontaneous. Cu is less reactive than H ⇒ doesn't displace H₂ from acid.

items.question: Will the reaction Zn + 2H⁺ → Zn²⁺ + H₂ occur spontaneously? (E°(Zn²⁺/Zn) = −0.76 V; E°(2H⁺/H₂) = 0.00 V.)
items.expectedAnswer: Yes. Zn is oxidised (anode, −0.76 V) and H⁺ is reduced (cathode, 0.00 V). E°_cell = 0 − (−0.76) = +0.76 V (POSITIVE) ⇒ SPONTANEOUS. Zn does react with dilute acid to produce H₂ gas.
items.explanation: Zn is more reactive than H ⇒ displaces H₂ from acid. Standard 'reactive metal in acid' demo.

items.question: In a galvanic cell with two half-cells, the voltmeter shows a POSITIVE reading. What does this indicate?
items.expectedAnswer: A positive voltmeter reading indicates that the cell reaction (as set up) is SPONTANEOUS — the polarities are correctly identified (cathode on the side connected to the voltmeter's positive terminal). E°_cell = +ve.
items.explanation: Positive voltmeter reading = spontaneous direction. Reversing the cell would give a negative reading.

items.question: Calculate the EMF of the cell Mg | Mg²⁺ || Ag⁺ | Ag. (E°(Mg²⁺/Mg) = −2.38 V; E°(Ag⁺/Ag) = +0.80 V.)
items.explanation: Mg is anode (more negative E°). Ag is cathode. E°_cell = 0.80 − (−2.38) = +3.18 V. (A high-EMF cell.)

items.question: Why does CHANGING the concentration of an electrolyte ABOVE 1 M (or temperature ABOVE 25°C) change the cell EMF from the standard E° value?
items.expectedAnswer: Standard electrode potentials are defined at 1 mol·dm⁻³ concentrations and 25°C. Deviation from these conditions shifts the equilibrium (Nernst equation): higher concentration of the reactant ⇒ stronger oxidising or reducing capability for that half-cell ⇒ EMF deviates from E°.
items.explanation: Non-standard conditions ⇒ Nernst equation applies; cell EMF deviates from tabulated E°.

items.question: Predict whether the following reaction will occur spontaneously at standard conditions: Cu²⁺ + 2Ag → Cu + 2Ag⁺. (E°(Cu²⁺/Cu) = +0.34 V; E°(Ag⁺/Ag) = +0.80 V.)
items.expectedAnswer: Cu²⁺ would be reduced (cathode, +0.34 V) and Ag would be oxidised (anode, +0.80 V). E°_cell = 0.34 − 0.80 = −0.46 V (NEGATIVE) ⇒ NON-SPONTANEOUS. Silver does NOT reduce Cu²⁺. The reverse reaction (Cu + Ag⁺ → Ag + Cu²⁺) is spontaneous.
items.explanation: Negative E°_cell ⇒ non-spontaneous. Ag is less reactive than Cu, so cannot displace Cu²⁺.

items.question: What does a HIGH POSITIVE E°_cell (e.g. > 2 V) tell you practically about a galvanic cell?
items.expectedAnswer: It indicates a strongly spontaneous reaction that can supply a relatively large voltage to an external circuit. The cell delivers significant electrical energy per coulomb of charge. Practical batteries (e.g. lithium-ion: ~3.7 V; alkaline: ~1.5 V; lead-acid: ~2 V per cell) use these reactions. Higher EMF = more useful electrical output (at standard conditions).
items.explanation: High E° ⇒ strongly spontaneous ⇒ useful voltage for batteries.

_error_signal_vocabulary.ERR_ANODE_FROM_E: Wrong anode/cathode assignment from E° values

_error_signal_vocabulary.ERR_EMF_SPONTANEITY: Doesn't link sign of E°_cell to spontaneity
_error_signal_vocabulary.ERR_SHE_REFERENCE: Doesn't use E°(SHE) = 0 V as reference
_error_signal_vocabulary.ERR_OXIDISING_STRENGTH_ORDER: Wrong order of oxidising-agent strength from E°
_error_signal_vocabulary.ERR_REDUCING_STRENGTH_ORDER: Wrong order of reducing-agent strength from E°
_error_signal_vocabulary.ERR_SIGN_FLIPPING: Incorrectly flips signs of E° values
_error_signal_vocabulary.ERR_DISPLACEMENT_PREDICTION: Wrong prediction of metal displacement from solution
_error_signal_vocabulary.ERR_NERNST: Doesn't recognise non-standard conditions require Nernst
